Called a **stoneback**, the creature is native to the tidal flats of a planet where gravity is ten times Earth’s. It is about a meter long, half a meter wide, and only fifteen centimeters tall. From a distance, it resembles a dark, wet paving stone moving with quiet determination.

Almost everything about it is built around that burden.

The stoneback has no neck, no slender waist, and nothing resembling a human knee. Its body is a broad oval beneath overlapping plates, with eight short limbs tucked along its sides.

The plates are not thick slabs of solid armor—that would add too much weight. Instead, they have a lightweight, honeycombed interior beneath a tough outer skin. Flexible seams let the animal bend around rocks without exposing much soft tissue.

Inside, its skeleton resembles a series of shallow bridge arches. Loads pass through several supports at once, so a single damaged limb does not leave half the animal hanging unsupported. Tough bands of connective tissue help hold its resting posture without continuous muscular effort.

Its underside carries a thick, ridged pad. When it stops, it lowers its belly onto the ground, taking the load off its legs entirely.

A resting stoneback looks less like an animal lying down than a building settling onto its foundations.

### How it moves

Each limb ends in a wide foot with gripping edges and a textured sole. The stoneback walks in a slow, overlapping sequence, usually keeping six or seven feet planted while the others advance.

It never jumps.

A fall of even a few body lengths could be disastrous, so it probes uncertain ground before committing its weight. Sensitive bristles around its feet detect loose gravel, soft mud, and the first movement of a slipping surface.

When frightened, it does not rear up or sprint. It flattens itself, hooks its feet into cracks, and draws its vulnerable limbs beneath the armor. On sediment, it can shovel itself into a shallow hollow until only its back remains visible.

In water it becomes surprisingly graceful. Buoyancy relieves much of its weight, and the same limbs that labor on land paddle it through shallow channels. Stonebacks spend much of their lives partly submerged, venturing onto exposed flats to feed.

High gravity makes moving blood upward expensive. The stoneback avoids much of that problem simply by being flat: its uppermost tissues are only a short distance above its lowest.

Its respiratory organs are folded chambers protected beneath the side plates. When the animal is exposed to air, muscular movements ventilate their moist internal surfaces. Underwater, separate frilled tissues extract dissolved oxygen.

The stoneback’s head is a broad wedge almost flush with its body. Four small eyes sit in armored recesses: two looking forward, two watching the sides.

Its world is mostly a narrow strip of horizon.

Vision matters, but touch and vibration matter more. Sensory pads beneath its jaw detect footsteps transmitted through wet ground. Short chemical feelers sweep the surface ahead, locating food and identifying the trails of other stonebacks.

Long antennae would be cumbersome and vulnerable, so its sensory structures are short, thick, and retractable.

To communicate, it presses a hard plate beneath its throat against the substrate and produces rhythmic tremors. A nearby stoneback feels the message through its feet: a territorial warning, a mating signal, or the low, repeated pulse of a parent gathering its young.

The stoneback grazes on tough microbial mats and low-growing, photosynthetic colonies coating the tidal rocks. A broad scraping mouth peels these layers away; internal grinding plates crush grit and shell fragments mixed into the meal.

It is also an opportunistic scavenger. A dead animal is valuable food, especially in a world where carrying a heavy body makes unnecessary travel costly.

Its metabolism is relatively slow, though not because high gravity automatically demands one. In its particular habitat, patient grazing and economical movement have proved more successful than constant pursuit.

The female carries a small clutch of large eggs in protected recesses beneath her side plates. She releases the hatchlings into shallow nursery pools, where buoyancy supports their still-soft bodies.

Young stonebacks are proportionally rounder and more aquatic than adults. Their skeletons strengthen gradually before they begin making longer trips onto exposed ground.

Parents guard the nursery by lying across its entrances: living barricades against small predators.

Up close, its armor is charcoal gray, streaked with rust-colored mineral deposits and thin green films of symbiotic microbes. Its movements are deliberate but not clumsy. Each foot tests, grips, and takes its share of the load.

If you crouched beside it, you might feel a faint tapping through your hand before you heard anything at all.

Then the stoneback would turn—not by lifting its head, but by shifting its whole armored body—and inspect you from a few centimeters above the ground.

It would not look like an Earth animal made stronger.

It would look like an animal for which **height itself had always been a hazard**.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
Call it a **stonecrawler**. From a distance, it looks like a dark, ridged boulder sliding through a field of moss. Only when it turns do you notice the eight feet beneath its rim—and the small, alert eyes watching you from armored recesses.

On a world with ten times Earth’s surface gravity, falling, standing, and even circulating blood become serious engineering problems. The stonecrawler’s body is built around one principle: **never lift anything higher than necessary.**

### Shape and structure

An adult is roughly eighty centimeters long, half a meter wide, and only ten centimeters tall. Its twenty-kilogram mass gives it approximately the same weight there as a two-hundred-kilogram animal on Earth.

Its body resembles a flattened tortoise crossed with a crab, but its shell is not a heavy dome. Instead, overlapping plates form a shallow, corrugated roof. Each plate has a hard mineral surface over a tough, fibrous interior, resisting cracks without requiring an enormous amount of material.

Underneath, a broad internal skeleton distributes forces through short struts. There is no long spine suspended between distant shoulders and hips. Almost every part of the body sits directly above a supporting limb or a padded section of belly.

At rest, the stonecrawler simply settles onto the ground.

### Legs and movement

Eight short legs project sideways, then bend beneath the body. Their load-bearing segments are thick and nearly vertical when planted; their joints have bony stops that help support weight without constant muscular effort.

The feet are broad, with gripping pads and small retractable claws. On soft ground, they spread. On rock, their edges conform to surface irregularities.

A walking stonecrawler moves with a slow, rippling gait, keeping most of its feet planted at any moment. It does not leap. It rarely climbs anything steeper than a gentle slope. Faced with a ledge, it tests the edge with its front feet and usually searches for another route.

Yet it is not helplessly sluggish. When threatened, it can make a brief, powerful scuttle, moving its feet rapidly while its body stays almost level.

### Circulation and breathing

Its organs lie side by side in a shallow layer rather than stacked vertically. That keeps the height difference between its circulatory pumps and its brain small, reducing the pressure needed to move blood against gravity.

Several muscular pumping chambers drive circulation through different regions of the body. One supplies the head, others the limbs and digestive tissues. Valves limit backflow when the animal tilts.

Breathing organs occupy protected cavities along its sides. Muscular bellows move air through closely folded exchange surfaces. The details would depend on the planet’s atmosphere—ten times Earth’s gravity does not, by itself, tell us how dense or oxygen-rich the air is.

### Senses and feeding

Its eyes sit close to ground level, giving it an intimate view of roots, stones, and other animals’ feet. It cannot see far across uneven terrain, so touch and vibration matter more than distant vision.

Sensitive pads beneath its body detect footsteps through the soil. Short, retractable feelers sample scents and probe crevices. An approaching animal might register as a sequence of faint tremors long before it becomes visible.

The mouth is underneath the front edge of the shell. Paired scraping jaws shave nutritious films from rocks and chew low-growing, leathery vegetation. It also eats carrion and small burrowing organisms. Food is pulled inward rather than lifted.

### Life on the ground

Stonecrawlers shelter in shallow burrows supported by dense root mats. They lay a few large, tough-skinned eggs in protected chambers; hatchlings emerge already low-slung and armored, because even a short tumble can be dangerous.

Their courtship is almost invisible: two animals rest beside one another, exchanging rhythmic taps through the ground. A receptive partner answers with the same pattern.

Up close, a stonecrawler would not seem like a monster crushed by gravity. It would seem exquisitely comfortable—**a living mosaic of armor, muscle, and sensitive feet, inhabiting the first ten centimeters above the soil as though that narrow space were the whole world.**
